claim: IgE can trigger potent allergic responses.
source: IgE can trigger potent allergic responses, yet the mechanisms regulating IgE production are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is part of established scientific knowledge about IgE function.

claim: The mechanisms regulating IgE production are poorly understood.
source: IgE can trigger potent allergic responses, yet the mechanisms regulating IgE production are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: IgE+ B cells are constrained by chronic activity of the IgE B cell receptor (BCR).
source: Here we reveal that IgE+ B cells are constrained by chronic activity of the IgE B cell receptor (BCR).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: In the absence of cognate antigen, the IgE BCR promoted terminal differentiation of B cells into plasma cells (PCs) under cell culture conditions mimicking T cell help.
source: In the absence of cognate antigen, the IgE BCR promoted terminal differentiation of B cells into plasma cells (PCs) under cell culture conditions mimicking T cell help.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Antigen-independent PC differentiation involved multiple IgE domains and Syk, CD19, BLNK, Btk, and IRF4.
source: This antigen-independent PC differentiation involved multiple IgE domains and Syk, CD19, BLNK, Btk, and IRF4.
evidence: This claim is supported by domain swap experiments (Figure 2) and genetic/pharmacological perturbation experiments (Figure 4).

claim: Disruption of BCR signaling in mice led to consistently exaggerated IgE+ germinal center (GC) B cell responses.
source: Disruption of BCR signaling in mice led to consistently exaggerated IgE+ germinal center (GC) B cell but variably increased PC responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments with multiple genetic and pharmacological perturbations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Disruption of BCR signaling in mice led to variably increased PC responses.
source: Disruption of BCR signaling in mice led to consistently exaggerated IgE+ germinal center (GC) B cell but variably increased PC responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The IgE BCR does not directly promote intrinsic apoptosis.
source: We were unable to confirm reports that the IgE BCR directly promoted intrinsic apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple apoptosis assays in cell culture and in vivo shown in Figure 6.

claim: IgE+ GC B cells exhibited poor antigen presentation.
source: Instead, IgE+ GC B cells exhibited poor antigen presentation and prolonged cell cycles, suggesting reduced competition for T cell help.
evidence: This claim is supported by Y-Ae antibody staining experiments shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: IgE+ GC B cells exhibited prolonged cell cycles.
source: Instead, IgE+ GC B cells exhibited poor antigen presentation and prolonged cell cycles, suggesting reduced competition for T cell help.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Poor antigen presentation and prolonged cell cycles suggest reduced competition for T cell help.
source: Instead, IgE+ GC B cells exhibited poor antigen presentation and prolonged cell cycles, suggesting reduced competition for T cell help.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings regarding antigen presentation and cell cycle.

claim: Chronic BCR activity and access to T cell help play critical roles in regulating IgE responses.
source: We propose that chronic BCR activity and access to T cell help play critical roles in regulating IgE responses.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity responses are typically localized to specific tissues such as the skin, nose, lung, or intestine.
source: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity responses are typically localized to specific tissues such as the skin, nose, lung, or intestine, whereas systemic responses can result in life-threatening anaphylaxis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IgE-mediated responses cited from the literature (Gould et al., 2003).

claim: Systemic IgE responses can result in life-threatening anaphylaxis.
source: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity responses are typically localized to specific tissues such as the skin, nose, lung, or intestine, whereas systemic responses can result in life-threatening anaphylaxis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IgE-mediated responses.

claim: Only a small fraction of individuals with allergic diseases will experience anaphylaxis.
source: Only a small fraction of individuals with allergic diseases will experience anaphylaxis, however, suggesting that IgE responses are normally restricted.
evidence: This is a clinical observation that supports the notion that IgE responses are regulated.

claim: IgE responses are normally restricted.
source: Only a small fraction of individuals with allergic diseases will experience anaphylaxis, however, suggesting that IgE responses are normally restricted.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical observation about anaphylaxis frequency.

claim: IgE is the least abundant antibody isotype in serum.
source: Indeed, IgE is the least abundant antibody isotype in serum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IgE abundance.

claim: The availability of IgE in serum is limited in part by a short half-life and binding to Fc receptors.
source: While the availability of IgE in serum is limited in part by a short half-life and binding to Fc receptors, the production of secreted IgE appears to be tightly regulated (Geha et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Geha et al., 2003).

claim: The production of secreted IgE appears to be tightly regulated.
source: While the availability of IgE in serum is limited in part by a short half-life and binding to Fc receptors, the production of secreted IgE appears to be tightly regulated (Geha et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement from the literature cited (Geha et al., 2003).

claim: Fluorescent IgE reporter mice have been generated to overcome challenges in studying IgE+ B cells.
source: These challenges have largely been overcome by the generation of fluorescent IgE reporter mice as well as improved technical methods (He et al., 2013; Talay et al., 2012a; Wesemann et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about technical advances cited from multiple studies.

claim: IgE+ B cells appeared only transiently and at low frequencies in germinal centers (GCs).
source: IgE+ B cells appeared only transiently and at low frequencies in germinal centers (GCs) (He et al., 2013; Talay et al., 2012b; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies cited.

claim: Germinal centers are major sites for antibody affinity maturation as well as the generation of long-lived plasma cells (PCs) and memory B cells.
source: These structures form during immune responses in lymphoid tissues and are major sites for antibody affinity maturation as well as the generation of long-lived plasma cells (PCs) and memory B cells (Allen et al., 2007a; Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about germinal centers cited from the literature.

claim: IgE+ responses typically exhibit reduced affinity maturation compared with IgG1+ responses.
source: Consistent with the limited participation of IgE+ B cells in GCs, IgE+ responses typically exhibit reduced affinity maturation compared with IgG1+ responses, and most of the affinity maturation that does occur requires an IgG1+ B cell intermediate (Erazo et al., 2007; He et al., 2013; Xiong et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from multiple previous studies cited.

claim: Most of the affinity maturation in IgE+ responses requires an IgG1+ B cell intermediate.
source: Consistent with the limited participation of IgE+ B cells in GCs, IgE+ responses typically exhibit reduced affinity maturation compared with IgG1+ responses, and most of the affinity maturation that does occur requires an IgG1+ B cell intermediate (Erazo et al., 2007; He et al., 2013; Xiong et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from multiple previous studies cited.

claim: There is a relative paucity of long-lived IgE+ PCs.
source: In addition, we observed a relative paucity of long-lived IgE+ PCs (Yang et al., 2012) and other groups reported that memory IgE responses were largely initiated by non-IgE-expressing B cells (He et al., 2013; Katona et al., 1991; Turqueti-Neves et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors cited.

claim: Memory IgE responses were largely initiated by non-IgE-expressing B cells.
source: In addition, we observed a relative paucity of long-lived IgE+ PCs (Yang et al., 2012) and other groups reported that memory IgE responses were largely initiated by non-IgE-expressing B cells (He et al., 2013; Katona et al., 1991; Turqueti-Neves et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from multiple previous studies cited.

claim: IgE+ B cells undergo an abortive GC phase that limits downstream IgE responses.
source: Taken together, it appears that IgE+ B cells undergo an abortive GC phase that limits downstream IgE responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cited findings about IgE+ B cell behavior in GCs.

claim: A larger proportion of IgE+ B cells have a PC phenotype compared with IgG1+ B cells.
source: In contrast, a larger proportion of IgE+ B cells were observed to have a PC phenotype compared with IgG1+ B cells in several studies (note that here we use a broad definition of PCs to refer to all antibody secreting cells, including plasmablasts) (Erazo et al., 2007; He et al., 2013; Laffleur et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from multiple previous studies cited.

claim: The increased PC differentiation of IgE+ B cells can be recapitulated in cell culture of primary mouse B cells.
source: We reported that this observation could be recapitulated in cell culture of primary mouse B cells, suggesting the increased PC differentiation of IgE+ B cells was B cell intrinsic (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors cited.

claim: The increased PC differentiation of IgE+ B cells is B cell intrinsic.
source: We reported that this observation could be recapitulated in cell culture of primary mouse B cells, suggesting the increased PC differentiation of IgE+ B cells was B cell intrinsic (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation from a previous study by the authors cited.

claim: The propensity of IgE+ B cells to undergo terminal differentiation into PCs may directly contribute to the low frequency and disappearance of IgE+ B cells from GCs.
source: We proposed that the propensity of IgE+ B cells to undergo terminal differentiation into PCs may directly contribute to the low frequency and disappearance of IgE+ B cells from GCs (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed model from a previous study by the authors cited.

claim: IgE+ GC B cells exhibit diminished BCR signaling and undergo increased rates of apoptosis.
source: Another group proposed that IgE+ GC B cells exhibit diminished BCR signaling and undergo increased rates of apoptosis (He et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed model from another group's study cited.

claim: Each isotype of BCR has a different constant region sequence which may confer different signaling capabilities.
source: Each isotype of BCR has a different constant region sequence which may confer different signaling capabilities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BCR structure and function.

claim: IgG BCRs can promote enhanced responses compared with IgM BCRs, most notably enhanced PC differentiation in recall responses.
source: IgG BCRs can promote enhanced responses compared with IgM BCRs, most notably enhanced PC differentiation in recall responses (Martin and Goodnow, 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study cited.

claim: The enhanced responses of IgG BCRs are thought to be due, at least in part, to the extended intracellular cytoplasmic tail of the IgG BCR, compared with the short three amino acid sequence (KVK) in IgM.
source: This is thought to be due, at least in part, to the extended intracellular cytoplasmic tail of the IgG BCR, compared with the short three amino acid sequence (KVK) in IgM (Martin and Goodnow, 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation from a previous study cited.

claim: A conserved tyrosine motif in the cytoplasmic tail of the IgG BCR is primarily responsible for its differential signaling.
source: A conserved tyrosine motif in the cytoplasmic tail of the IgG BCR, which was reported to be primarily responsible for its differential signaling, is also present in the IgE BCR (Engels et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study cited.

claim: The conserved tyrosine motif is also present in the IgE BCR.
source: A conserved tyrosine motif in the cytoplasmic tail of the IgG BCR, which was reported to be primarily responsible for its differential signaling, is also present in the IgE BCR (Engels et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study cited.

claim: The cytoplasmic tail of the IgE BCR has been implicated in promoting apoptosis through binding the mitochondrial protein Hax1.
source: The cytoplasmic tail of the IgE BCR has also been implicated in promoting apoptosis through binding the mitochondrial protein Hax1 (Laffleur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study cited.

claim: In the presence of T cell help signals, the IgE BCR promoted PC differentiation.
source: Here we show that the IgE BCR is a major determinant of IgE+ B cell fate. In the presence of T cell help signals, the IgE BCR promoted PC differentiation.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: IgE BCR-mediated cell fate predisposition occurred in the absence of cognate antigen.
source: This cell fate predisposition occurred in the absence of cognate antigen, whereas the IgG1 BCR promoted PC differentiation only in the presence of cognate antigen.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The IgG1 BCR promoted PC differentiation only in the presence of cognate antigen.
source: This cell fate predisposition occurred in the absence of cognate antigen, whereas the IgG1 BCR promoted PC differentiation only in the presence of cognate antigen.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Multiple domains of the BCRs were responsible for the difference between the IgE and IgG1 isotypes.
source: Multiple domains of the BCRs were responsible for the difference between the IgE and IgG1 isotypes.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by domain swap experiments in Figure 2.

claim: The propensity of the IgE BCR to induce antigen-independent PC differentiation was associated with a weak, constitutive activity of the IgE BCR.
source: The propensity of the IgE BCR to induce antigen-independent PC differentiation was associated with a weak, constitutive activity of the IgE BCR.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by experiments in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Genetic or pharmacological perturbations in BCR signaling led to reduced PC differentiation of IgE+ B cells in the absence of cognate antigen in cell culture.
source: Genetic or pharmacological perturbations in BCR signaling led to reduced PC differentiation of IgE+ B cells in the absence of cognate antigen in cell culture.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Reductions in BCR signaling led to consistently increased IgE+ GC B cell responses with variable effects on PCs in immunized mice.
source: In immunized mice, reductions in BCR signaling led to consistently increased IgE+ GC B cell responses with variable effects on PCs.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by in vivo experiments in Figure 5.

claim: BCR signaling slowed the cell cycle progression of IgE+ GC B cells.
source: Instead, BCR signaling slowed the cell cycle progression of IgE+ GC B cells, and low IgE BCR expression limited antigen uptake and presentation.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by experiments in Figure 7.

claim: Low IgE BCR expression limited antigen uptake and presentation.
source: Instead, BCR signaling slowed the cell cycle progression of IgE+ GC B cells, and low IgE BCR expression limited antigen uptake and presentation.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by experiments in Figure 7.

claim: IgE B cell responses are restrained by a predisposition toward early PC differentiation, prolonged cell cycles, and limited access to T cell help, leading to reduced affinity maturation and memory cell generation.
source: Thus, IgE B cell responses are restrained by a predisposition toward early PC differentiation, prolonged cell cycles, and limited access to T cell help, leading to reduced affinity maturation and memory cell generation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: A substantially greater fraction of IgE+ cells were PCs compared with IgG1+ cells in primary B cell cultures with anti-CD40 antibodies and IL-4.
source: In these B cell cultures, a substantially greater fraction of IgE+ cells were PCs compared with IgG1+ cells. This result was confirmed again here using CD138 (Syndecan-1) as a marker of PCs (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: A larger fraction of IgE+ cells than IgG1+ cells had a PC phenotype regardless of the concentration of anti-CD40 antibody.
source: We found that a larger fraction of IgE+ cells than IgG1+ cells had a PC phenotype regardless of the concentration of anti-CD40 antibody, although we noted that stronger CD40 stimulation was inhibitory toward PC differentiation (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Stronger CD40 stimulation was inhibitory toward PC differentiation.
source: We found that a larger fraction of IgE+ cells than IgG1+ cells had a PC phenotype regardless of the concentration of anti-CD40 antibody, although we noted that stronger CD40 stimulation was inhibitory toward PC differentiation (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The increased PC differentiation occurs in IgE+ B cells that have undergone the same number of cell divisions as IgG1+ B cells.
source: We also previously established that the increased PC differentiation occurs in IgE+ B cells that have undergone the same number of cell divisions as IgG1+ B cells (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors cited.

claim: Among all isotypes tested, the IgE BCR promoted the highest frequency of PC differentiation in the absence of cognate antigen.
source: Strikingly, among all isotypes tested, the IgE BCR promoted the highest frequency of PC differentiation in the absence of cognate antigen (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data of retrovirally transduced B cells shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The IgM and IgG1 BCRs did not promote PC differentiation in the absence of cognate antigen.
source: The IgM and IgG1 BCRs did not promote PC differentiation in the absence of cognate antigen, whereas the IgD and IgA BCRs had intermediate effects (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The IgD and IgA BCRs had intermediate effects on PC differentiation in the absence of cognate antigen.
source: The IgM and IgG1 BCRs did not promote PC differentiation in the absence of cognate antigen, whereas the IgD and IgA BCRs had intermediate effects (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Upon the addition of TNP-OVA, the TNP-specific IgG1 BCR promoted robust PC differentiation, similar to the IgE BCR.
source: Upon the addition of TNP-ovalbumin (OVA), the TNP-specific IgG1 BCR promoted robust PC differentiation, similar to the IgE BCR (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The addition of TNP-OVA resulted in a more moderate increase in PC differentiation in cells transduced with TNP-specific IgM BCRs.
source: The addition of TNP-OVA also resulted in a more moderate increase in PC differentiation in cells transduced with TNP-specific IgM BCRs, with intermediate results with IgD BCRs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The addition of TNP-OVA did not cause a further increase in PC differentiation in cells transduced with TNP-specific IgE or IgA BCRs.
source: However, the addition of TNP-OVA did not cause a further increase in PC differentiation in cells transduced with TNP-specific IgE or IgA BCRs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The IgE BCR is a strong inducer of PC differentiation in an antigen-independent manner, mimicking the behavior of an antigen-engaged IgG1 BCR.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the IgE BCR is a strong inducer of PC differentiation in an antigen-independent manner, mimicking the behavior of an antigen-engaged IgG1 BCR.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings in Figure 1.

claim: Antigen-independent PC differentiation was unaffected when the IgE CT was replaced with that of IgG1.
source: Surprisingly, antigen-independent PC differentiation was unaffected when the IgE CT was replaced with that of IgG1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data of domain swap experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Swapping the TM region had no impact on antigen-independent PC differentiation.
source: The transmembrane (TM) region of the BCR is thought to mediate association with the signaling adapters Igα and Igβ (Reth, 1992), yet swapping the TM region also had no impact on antigen-independent PC differentiation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data of domain swap experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The expression of constructs in which the migis of IgE was swapped with that of IgG1 led to a profound loss of antigen-independent PC differentiation.
source: The expression of constructs in which the migis of IgE was swapped with that of IgG1 led to a profound loss of antigen-independent PC differentiation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data of domain swap experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The IgE migis region appears to be necessary, but not sufficient, for antigen-independent PC differentiation mediated by the IgE BCR.
source: Taken together, the IgE migis region appears to be necessary, but not sufficient, for antigen-independent PC differentiation mediated by the IgE BCR.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the domain swap experiments in Figure 2A.

claim: Full antigen-independent activity of the IgE BCR required the IgE migis region to be combined with either the extracellular domains of IgE or the CT of IgE.
source: Full antigen-independent activity of the IgE BCR required the IgE migis region to be combined with either the extracellular domains of IgE or the CT of IgE.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the domain swap experiments in Figure 2A.

claim: IgM was downmodulated in B cells transduced with IgE but not with IgG1.
source: We observed that IgM was downmodulated in B cells transduced with IgE (Figure 2B, construct 1) but not with IgG1 (Figure 2B, construct 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The IgM downmodulation was dependent on the migis region.
source: The IgM downmodulation was dependent on the migis region, as revealed by transducing constructs with the migis regions swapped (Figure 2B, constructs 2 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All of the constructs that contained the IgE migis resulted in downmodulation of surface IgM, whereas the constructs that contained the IgG1 migis did not.
source: Indeed, in cells transduced with each of the constructs shown in Figure 2A, all of the constructs that contained the IgE migis resulted in downmodulation of surface IgM, whereas the constructs that contained the IgG1 migis did not (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The IgE BCR depends on binding to Igα for export from the endoplasmic reticulum, whereas the IgG BCR does not.
source: It was reported that similar to IgM, the IgE BCR depends on binding to Igα for export from the endoplasmic reticulum, whereas the IgG BCR does not (Venkitaraman et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study cited.

claim: The IgE migis made BCR surface expression completely dependent on Igα, whereas the IgG1 migis permitted substantial surface BCR localization in the absence of Igα.
source: Remarkably, the IgE migis made BCR surface expression completely dependent on Igα, whereas the IgG1 migis permitted substantial surface BCR localization in the absence of Igα (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data of J558L cells shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The migis region is a major site of interaction with Igα.
source: These data indicate that the migis region is a major site of interaction with Igα.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings in Figure 2D and E.

claim: In B1-8flox/+ Cγ1Cre/+ cells, the IgE migis region still contributed to antigen-independent PC differentiation, but played a less prominent role than in the AID-deficient B cells.
source: In domain swap experiments in B1-8flox/+ Cγ1Cre/+ cells, the IgE migis region still contributed to antigen-independent PC differentiation, but played a less prominent role than in the AID-deficient B cells, presumably since no IgM was present to compete for Igα (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both the IgE CH2 and IgE CH3 reproducibly contributed to antigen-independent PC differentiation.
source: Indeed, both the IgE CH2 and IgE CH3 reproducibly contributed to antigen-independent PC differentiation, as revealed by transducing hybrid constructs in which these domains had been swapped with the IgG1 hinge and CH2, respectively (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Multiple parts of the IgE molecule, specifically the CH2, CH3, migis, and CT, all contribute to antigen-independent PC differentiation.
source: Thus, multiple parts of the IgE molecule, specifically the CH2, CH3, migis, and CT, all contribute to antigen-independent PC differentiation, making this BCR distinct from the IgG1 BCR.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the domain swap experiments in Figure 2.

claim: The surface expression of the transduced IgE and IgG1 BCRs were equivalent to each other.
source: The surface expression of the transduced IgE and IgG1 BCRs were equivalent to each other, as measured with an antibody to the light chain which pairs with these heavy chains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The surface expression of the transduced BCRs was overlapping with the surface expression of normal endogenous IgE BCRs, but less than that of normal endogenous IgG1 BCRs.
source: We observed that the surface expression of the transduced BCRs was overlapping with the surface expression of normal endogenous IgE BCRs, but less than that of normal endogenous IgG1 BCRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Membrane IgE normally has lower expression than membrane IgG1.
source: This difference was due to the fact that membrane IgE normally has lower expression than membrane IgG1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), as previously reported (He et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and cited from a previous study.

claim: A larger fraction of IgE+ B cells than IgG1+ B cells expressed the activation marker CD69.
source: We found that a larger fraction of IgE+ B cells than IgG1+ B cells expressed the activation marker CD69 (Figure 3A), which was particularly apparent with low concentrations of anti-CD40 antibody, since strong CD40 stimulation could itself promote CD69 upregulation (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IgE+ B cells had higher constitutive Nur77 expression than IgG1+ B cells.
source: IgE+ B cells had higher constitutive Nur77 expression than IgG1+ B cells, as revealed by a Nur77-GFP reporter (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The elevated CD69 and Nur77 expression suggest that IgE+ B cells have higher constitutive BCR activity than IgG1+ B cells.
source: The elevated CD69 and Nur77 expression suggest that IgE+ B cells have higher constitutive BCR activity than IgG1+ B cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Some of the IgE BCR clusters were noticeably higher in fluorescence intensity and tended to be larger in size than the IgG1 BCR clusters.
source: However, some of the IgE BCR clusters were noticeably higher in fluorescence intensity (Figures 3C, D and E) and tended to be larger in size (Figure 3F) than the IgG1 BCR clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figures 3C-F.

claim: IgE BCRs intrinsically form more prominent clusters compared with IgG1 BCRs in quiescent B cells.
source: These results suggest that IgE BCRs intrinsically form more prominent clusters compared with IgG1 BCRs in quiescent B cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the TIRF microscopy data in Figure 3C-F.

claim: The Brownian diffusion of IgE BCRs was more confined compared to that of IgG1 BCRs.
source: This tracking analysis illuminated that the Brownian diffusion of IgE BCRs was more confined compared to that of IgG1 BCRs (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by single molecule tracking data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: IgE BCRs have decreased Brownian diffusion coefficients compared with IgG1 BCRs.
source: Moreover, the short-range diffusion coefficients of single BCR molecules were processed and derived into a cumulative distribution probability plot, which confirmed that IgE BCRs have decreased Brownian diffusion coefficients compared with IgG1 BCRs (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by single molecule tracking data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: IgE BCRs form more prominent clusters with reduced mobility compared with IgG1 BCRs in the absence of cognate antigen.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that IgE BCRs form more prominent clusters with reduced mobility compared with IgG1 BCRs in the absence of cognate antigen, providing further evidence that these BCRs differ in their constitutive activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the TIRF microscopy and single molecule tracking data in Figure 3.

claim: Treatment of the primary B cell cultures with ibrutinib to inhibit Btk led to reduced antigen-independent PC differentiation.
source: Treatment of the primary B cell cultures with ibrutinib to inhibit Btk, an important kinase in BCR signaling, led to reduced antigen-independent PC differentiation (Figure 4A), while cell viability and CSR were maintained (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Syk heterozygosity led to reduced PC differentiation in the absence of antigen.
source: Syk heterozygosity led to reduced PC differentiation in the absence of antigen (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Antigen-independent PC differentiation was completely abrogated in CD19-deficient B cells.
source: Strikingly, antigen-independent PC differentiation was completely abrogated in CD19-deficient B cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: BLNK only partially contributed to antigen-independent PC differentiation, with a two-fold reduction observed in BLNK-deficient B cells.
source: In contrast, the BCR signaling adapter BLNK (BASH, SLP-65) only partially contributed to antigen-independent PC differentiation, with a two-fold reduction observed in BLNK-deficient B cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Antigen-independent PC differentiation has a differential reliance on particular BCR signaling pathways.
source: These results suggest that antigen-independent PC differentiation has a differential reliance on particular BCR signaling pathways.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential effects of various signaling perturbations in Figure 4.

claim: BCR signaling is needed for antigen-independent PC differentiation.
source: Taken together, these data in general demonstrate that BCR signaling is needed for antigen-independent PC differentiation, providing further evidence that this is mediated by constitutive activity of the IgE BCR.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings in Figure 4.

claim: Ibrutinib treatment reduced antigen-independent PC differentiation mediated by the transduced BCRs.
source: In the absence of TNP-OVA, ibrutinib treatment reduced antigen-independent PC differentiation mediated by the transduced BCRs, as we had previously observed in normal primary B cells that had undergone natural class switch recombination to IgE and IgG1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: When TNP-OVA was added, antigen-dependent PC differentiation was not significantly affected by ibrutinib treatment.
source: Interestingly, however, when we added TNP-OVA, antigen-dependent PC differentiation was not significantly affected by ibrutinib treatment (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Ibrutinib treatment abrogated Nur77-GFP expression in the absence of antigen.
source: Ibrutinib treatment abrogated Nur77-GFP expression in the absence of antigen, whereas ibrutinib treatment had less pronounced effects on Nur77-GFP expression in the presence of antigen (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Ibrutinib treatment had less pronounced effects on Nur77-GFP expression in the presence of antigen.
source: Ibrutinib treatment abrogated Nur77-GFP expression in the absence of antigen, whereas ibrutinib treatment had less pronounced effects on Nur77-GFP expression in the presence of antigen (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The constitutive activity of the IgE BCR is weaker than antigen-dependent BCR stimulation and is more sensitive to pharmacological inhibition.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the constitutive activity of the IgE BCR is weaker than antigen-dependent BCR stimulation and is more sensitive to pharmacological inhibition.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings in Figure 4E and F.

claim: BLNK-deficient mice showed a striking increase in IgE+ B cell frequencies within GCs, compared with no change in IgG1+ B cell frequencies.
source: After immunization, BLNK-deficient mice showed a striking increase in IgE+ B cell frequencies within GCs, compared with no change in IgG1+ B cell frequencies, in the context of relatively normal total GC B cell numbers (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BLNK-deficient mice had an increase in IgE+ PCs, but not IgG1+ PCs.
source: BLNK-deficient mice also had an increase in IgE+ PCs, but not IgG1+ PCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cd19 heterozygous mice showed a selective increase in the frequency of IgE+ B cells in GCs, but did not affect the frequency of IgG1+ B cells nor total GC B cell numbers.
source: The two-fold reduction in Cd19 in these mice also resulted in a selective increase in the frequency of IgE+ B cells in GCs, but did not affect the frequency of IgG1+ B cells nor total GC B cell numbers (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cd19 heterozygous mice showed a modest elevation in IgE+ PCs.
source: Cd19 heterozygous mice also showed a modest elevation in IgE+ PCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ibrutinib treatment during an ongoing GC response resulted in a general two-fold reduction in GC cell numbers.
source: This inhibition of BCR signaling during an ongoing GC response resulted in a general two-fold reduction in GC cell numbers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) as previously reported (Mueller et al., 2015), but there was again a selective increase in the frequency of IgE+ B cells in GCs, whereas the frequency of IgG1+ GC B cells was unaffected (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and cited from a previous study.

claim: Ibrutinib treatment resulted in a selective increase in the frequency of IgE+ B cells in GCs, whereas the frequency of IgG1+ GC B cells was unaffected.
source: This inhibition of BCR signaling during an ongoing GC response resulted in a general two-fold reduction in GC cell numbers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) as previously reported (Mueller et al., 2015), but there was again a selective increase in the frequency of IgE+ B cells in GCs, whereas the frequency of IgG1+ GC B cells was unaffected (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A two-fold decrease in Syk specifically in activated B cells resulted in a selective increase in the frequency of IgE+ B cells within GCs, whereas IgG1+ B cell frequencies were not significantly affected.
source: This two-fold decrease in Syk specifically in activated B cells also resulted in a selective increase in the frequency of IgE+ B cells within GCs, whereas IgG1+ B cell frequencies were not significantly affected, in the context of slightly elevated total GC B cell numbers (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IgE+ PCs, but not IgG1+ PCs, were elevated when activated B cells were Syk heterozygous.
source: IgE+ PCs, but not IgG1+ PCs, were elevated as well when activated B cells were Syk heterozygous (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: With four different BCR signaling perturbations, IgE+ B cell frequencies were selectively elevated in GCs.
source: Thus, with four different BCR signaling perturbations, IgE+ B cell frequencies were selectively elevated in GCs, indicating that in general, BCR signaling negatively regulates IgE+ GC B cell responses.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the in vivo experiments in Figure 5.

claim: BCR signaling negatively regulates IgE+ GC B cell responses.
source: Thus, with four different BCR signaling perturbations, IgE+ B cell frequencies were selectively elevated in GCs, indicating that in general, BCR signaling negatively regulates IgE+ GC B cell responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the in vivo experiments in Figure 5.

claim: A single copy of Irf4 was conditionally deleted in activated B cells from Irf4flox/+ Cγ1Cre/+ mice.
source: A single copy of Irf4 was conditionally deleted in activated B cells from Irf4flox/+ Cγ1Cre/+ mice.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: Cell culture of Irf4-heterozygous B cells reduced the antigen-independent PC differentiation of IgE+ B cells.
source: Cell culture of Irf4-heterozygous B cells reduced the antigen-independent PC differentiation of IgE+ B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), similar to our BCR signaling perturbations in Figure 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Irf4 heterozygosity resulted in a two-fold increase in the frequency of IgE+ B cells compared with a 10% increase in the frequency of IgG1+ B cells in GCs.
source: In vivo, the effects of Irf4 heterozygosity were subtle, but we observed a two-fold increase in the frequency of IgE+ B cells compared with a 10% increase in the frequency of IgG1+ B cells in GCs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Irf4 may be one target responsible for the specific effects of BCR signaling on IgE GC and PC responses.
source: These findings suggest that Irf4 may be one target responsible for the specific effects of BCR signaling on IgE GC and PC responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings with Irf4 heterozygous mice.

claim: The majority of IgE+ and IgG1+ GC B cells carried somatic mutations.
source: The majority of IgE+ and IgG1+ GC B cells carried somatic mutations, as expected, whereas the vast majority of IgE+ and IgG1+ PCs had germline sequences at this timepoint (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The vast majority of IgE+ and IgG1+ PCs had germline sequences at this timepoint.
source: The majority of IgE+ and IgG1+ GC B cells carried somatic mutations, as expected, whereas the vast majority of IgE+ and IgG1+ PCs had germline sequences at this timepoint (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of IgE+ PCs were likely derived from the extrafollicular pathway.
source: This result indicates that the majority of IgE+ PCs were likely derived from the extrafollicular pathway, suggesting that a two-fold reduction in Syk led to an increase in the IgE+ PC extrafollicular response.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the sequence analysis data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: BCR signaling is implicated in the regulation of both extrafollicular and GC pathways of the IgE response.
source: Overall, our data implicate BCR signaling in the regulation of both extrafollicular and GC pathways of the IgE response.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the in vivo experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Withdrawal of anti-CD40 and/or IL-4 led to a general increase in apoptotic cells.
source: While withdrawal of anti-CD40 and/or IL-4 led to a general increase in apoptotic cells as measured by annexinV staining, the frequency of apoptotic IgE+ and IgG1+ B cells were similar (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The frequency of apoptotic IgE+ and IgG1+ B cells were similar upon withdrawal of anti-CD40 and/or IL-4.
source: While withdrawal of anti-CD40 and/or IL-4 led to a general increase in apoptotic cells as measured by annexinV staining, the frequency of apoptotic IgE+ and IgG1+ B cells were similar (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ectopic expression of the IgE BCR in primary B cells resulted in similar frequencies of apoptosis to ectopic expression of the IgG1 BCR.
source: Ectopic expression of the IgE BCR in primary B cells also resulted in similar frequencies of apoptosis to ectopic expression of the IgG1 BCR (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Swapping or truncating the IgE CT domain had no significant impact on apoptosis.
source: Swapping (constructs 2 and 5) or truncating the IgE CT domain to the short KVK sequence found in IgM (construct 3) also had no significant impact on apoptosis (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Similar frequencies of apoptosis were observed in WEHI-231 cells transduced with the IgE BCR versus IgG1 BCR or with CT mutant constructs.
source: Similar frequencies of apoptosis were observed in WEHI-231 cells transduced with the IgE BCR versus IgG1 BCR or with CT mutant constructs (Figure 6D), as we had observed in primary B cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The frequency of cells transduced with the IgE BCR was stable from 3 d to 7 d after transduction.
source: The frequency of cells transduced with the IgE BCR was also stable from 3 d to 7 d after transduction (Figure 6D), arguing against any deleterious effects of expressing the IgE BCR or its CT.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Similar frequencies of apoptosis were found among IgE+ and IgG1+ GC B cells when stained with an active caspase-3 antibody.
source: However, when we stained with an active caspase-3 antibody, we found similar frequencies of apoptosis among IgE+ and IgG1+ GC B cells (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Similar rates of apoptosis were observed when cells were incubated with an active caspase substrate and stained with annexin V.
source: We also observed similar rates of apoptosis when we incubated the cells with an active caspase substrate and when we stained the cells with annexin V (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: There is no evidence that the IgE BCR directly promotes intrinsic apoptosis in primary B cells in culture, in B cell lines, nor in vivo GC B cells.
source: Taken together, we find no evidence that the IgE BCR directly promotes intrinsic apoptosis in primary B cells in culture, in B cell lines, nor in vivo GC B cells.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the apoptosis experiments in Figure 6.

claim: IgE+ B cells were lost from GCs at a similar rate in Bcl2 transgenic mice and littermate controls.
source: IgE+ B cells were lost from GCs at a similar rate in Bcl2 transgenic mice and littermate controls (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The data are inconsistent with the model that IgE+ B cells are eliminated from GCs primarily due to increased rates of intrinsic apoptosis mediated by the IgE BCR.
source: Taken together, our data are inconsistent with the model that IgE+ B cells are eliminated from GCs primarily due to increased rates of intrinsic apoptosis mediated by the IgE BCR.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the apoptosis experiments in Figure 6.

claim: IgE+ GC B cells tended to have slower cell cycles than IgG1+ GC B cells.
source: In wild-type mice, we observed that IgE+ GC B cells tended to have slower cell cycles than IgG1+ GC B cells, as revealed by a smaller proportion of EdU+ cells reaching the G1 phase of the cell cycle in this time window (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Ibrutinib treatment resulted in a greater fraction of EdU-labeled cells progressing to the G1 phase of the cell cycle in 3.5 hr, indicating faster cell cycles.
source: Interestingly, ibrutinib treatment resulted in a greater fraction of EdU-labeled cells progressing to the G1 phase of the cell cycle in 3.5 hr, indicating faster cell cycles (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In ibrutinib-treated mice, IgE+ and IgG1+ GC B cells showed equivalent cell cycle speeds.
source: In ibrutinib-treated mice, IgE+ and IgG1+ GC B cells showed equivalent cell cycle speeds (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Inhibiting BCR signaling made IgE+ GC B cells more competitive with IgG1+ GC B cells.
source: Thus, inhibiting BCR signaling actually made IgE+ GC B cells more competitive with IgG1+ GC B cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cell cycle experiments in Figure 7C.

claim: BCR signaling normally constrains IgE+ GC B cell responses through prolonged cell cycle times.
source: These data suggest that BCR signaling normally constrains IgE+ GC B cell responses through prolonged cell cycle times.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cell cycle experiments in Figure 7.

claim: Antigen-specific IgE+ GC B cells bound 4.4-fold less HEL than antigen-specific IgG1+ GC B cells.
source: We observed that antigen-specific IgE+ GC B cells bound 4.4-fold less HEL than antigen-specific IgG1+ GC B cells (Figure 7D and E), consistent with a four-fold difference reported with a different antigen system (He et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: IgE+ GC B cells had reduced Y-Ae antibody binding compared with IgG1+ GC B cells, indicating that IgE+ GC B cells displayed fewer peptide-MHC complexes.
source: After several hours, allowing time for antigen processing to occur, IgE+ GC B cells had reduced Y-Ae antibody binding compared with IgG1+ GC B cells, indicating that IgE+ GC B cells displayed fewer peptide-MHC complexes (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: The low BCR surface expression on IgE+ GC B cells limits the ability of these cells to compete for T cell help.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the low BCR surface expression on IgE+ GC B cells limits the ability of these cells to compete for T cell help, illuminating an additional mechanism by which the IgE BCR may limit IgE+ GC B cell responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the antigen uptake and presentation experiments in Figure 7.

claim: Distinct properties of the IgE BCR regulate the fate of IgE+ B cells.
source: The findings we have reported here establish that distinct properties of the IgE BCR regulate the fate of IgE+ B cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: The constitutive activity of the IgE BCR promoted PC differentiation in an antigen-independent manner in the presence of stimuli mimicking T cell help.
source: In the presence of stimuli mimicking T cell help, the constitutive activity of the IgE BCR promoted PC differentiation in an antigen-independent manner.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: The difference between the IgE and IgG1 BCRs was attributed to multiple domains, particularly the extracellular membrane-proximal migis region, with further contributions from the IgE CH2 and CH3 extracellular domains and the IgE CT.
source: This difference between the IgE and IgG1 BCRs was attributed to multiple domains, particularly the extracellular membrane-proximal migis region, with further contributions from the IgE CH2 and CH3 extracellular domains and the IgE CT.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the domain swap experiments.

claim: In cell culture, the BCR signaling adapters BLNK, Btk, CD19, and Syk contributed to antigen-independent PC differentiation mediated by the IgE BCR, with an essential role for CD19.
source: In cell culture, the BCR signaling adapters BLNK, Btk, CD19, and Syk contributed to antigen-independent PC differentiation mediated by the IgE BCR, with an essential role for CD19.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the signaling perturbation experiments in cell culture.

claim: In mice, genetic deficiency or pharmacological inhibition of BCR signaling components consistently resulted in elevated IgE GC responses, yet IgE PC responses were variably affected.
source: In mice, genetic deficiency or pharmacological inhibition of these signaling components consistently resulted in elevated IgE GC responses, yet IgE PC responses were variably affected.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the in vivo experiments.

claim: The increased IgE+ GC B cell responses upon Btk inhibition were associated with accelerated cell cycle progression.
source: The increased IgE+ GC B cell responses upon Btk inhibition were associated with accelerated cell cycle progression, suggesting that the reduced competitive fitness of IgE+ GC B cells is in part due to BCR signaling.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the cell cycle experiments.

claim: The reduced competitive fitness of IgE+ GC B cells is in part due to BCR signaling.
source: The increased IgE+ GC B cell responses upon Btk inhibition were associated with accelerated cell cycle progression, suggesting that the reduced competitive fitness of IgE+ GC B cells is in part due to BCR signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cell cycle experiments.

claim: Low surface expression of the IgE BCR on GC B cells led to reduced antigen uptake and presentation, likely limiting access to T cell help.
source: In addition, low surface expression of the IgE BCR on GC B cells led to reduced antigen uptake and presentation, likely limiting access to T cell help.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the antigen uptake and presentation experiments.
